title: Nepal floods: 5-year-old among three Indians rescued from Trishuli Bazaar area
author: PTI
content_html:
Three more Indian nationals, among them a five-year-old child, have been rescued from the flood-hit Trishuli Bazaar area of Nepal, bringing the total count of Indian evacuees to 169, while 275 nationals remain missing, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said on Friday (September 4, 2026).

Sharing broader updates on the safety of Indian nationals, MEA Spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal noted that 1,907 Indians have safely crossed over to Nepal from China.

Also read | Nepal floods: Indian volunteers take relief to isolated communities

The three Indian nationals rescued from the Trishuli Bazaar area have been identified as Abhijit Suresh Pawar, Dipika Abhijit Pawar, and five-year-old Samarth Abhijit Pawar, Mr. Jaiswal said, adding that the Indian Embassy in Kathmandu is facilitating their return flight home.

The spokesperson said India has supplied around 95 tonnes of relief material to Nepal since the flash floods hit the country on August 26.

The death toll from the floods has risen to at least 1,295 after rescue workers recovered more bodies from affected areas, according to Nepalese authorities.

While emergency teams have rescued more than 12,000 people, roughly 5,000 remain missing as search and rescue operations continue.

"As per our information, 275 Indian nationals remain missing. We continue to be in close touch with the Nepali government," Mr. Jaiswal said at his regular media briefing.

"We deeply appreciate the efforts of the Nepalese authorities in this regard." Mr. Jaiswal said 169 Indian nationals have been rescued and 1,907 Indians have safely crossed into Nepal from China.

"As per official sources in China, there are no Indian travellers who are stranded in the Tibetan Autonomous Region in China," Mr. Jaiswal noted.

The MEA spokesperson said India will continue to provide assistance to Nepal as per the requirements of the government in that country.

"We do plan to send more forensic kits, Bailey bridges and other materials that are requested by the government of Nepal," he said.

Mr. Jaiswal said India has supplied around 95 tonnes of relief material on seven aircraft to Nepal till now.

"In addition to the relief material, we have also sent 54 personnel to support relief and rescue efforts in Nepal. This comprises 30 tunnel rescue experts, 19 forensic experts, and a five-member medical team. Our rescue and forensic teams are deployed on the ground, and they are working closely with the Nepalese authorities," he said.

The first tranche of relief materials was sent by India hours after Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke to his Nepalese counterpart Balendra Shah on August 26, the day the flash floods struck the Himalayan nation.

Mr. Modi had assured Mr. Shah of all possible humanitarian assistance to deal with the situation.

The floods have damaged 35 motorable bridges, 45 suspension bridges, and 40 km of black-topped roads, mainly in central Nepal, according to local authorities.

Mr. Jaiswal said India responded promptly to the flash floods in Nepal and will continue to support the reconstruction and recovery efforts in the country.

title: Bihar reiterates parents’ salaries, agricultural income cannot be counted for OBC creamy layer
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:
The Bihar government has reiterated that officials in the State cannot include parents’ salaries and agricultural earnings when calculating income to determine the creamy layer status of Other Backward Classes (OBC) candidates.

In an order issued by the General Administration Department (GAD), the State government said that instructions issued by the Centre and the State on the income test stipulate this.

This comes in the backdrop of the Union government approaching the Supreme Court last week to seek clarity on how to apply the income test, especially in light of the top court’s March 11 Rohith Nathan judgment. Interestingly, in doing so, the Union government has also argued that in some cases, there may be a need to include salaries of parents to distinguish creamy layer candidates among OBC candidates.

In a September 1 order addressed to all District Magistrates, the Bihar government reiterated earlier orders on the creamy layer exclusion procedure for OBCs, specifically those concerning the application of the income test. However, the order does not explicitly mention the Rohith Nathan judgment or the issues that this judgment dealt with regarding the application of the income test.

The GAD referred to the 1993 principal guidelines of the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) governing the creamy layer exclusion process, and to orders issued by the State government since then. It acknowledged reports that the creamy layer exclusion process, as set out in these guidelines, was not being followed completely and called for strict adherence to them.

Rohith Nathan judgment

The Rohith Nathan judgment in March this year recognised that the DoPT was applying the income test of the creamy layer exclusion process differently for different categories of OBC candidates. The court had described this as “hostile discrimination”, where income from parents’ salaries alone had been used to exclude some OBC candidates from reservation.

The court made it clear that the creamy layer exclusion was meant to remove OBC candidates who had acquired certain social and economic privileges. Using only economic criteria to exclude OBCs from reservation was not in line with the foundational principles of the creamy layer exclusion tool. It thus asked the Centre to create supernumerary posts for the litigant candidates and adjust them in the Civil Services accordingly.

However, months after this judgment, the Centre filed applications in the Supreme Court, arguing that it is “extremely difficult” to apply its ruling retrospectively, but also sought clarity on the income test itself, even arguing that in some cases, income from salaries should be considered because it might be the “sole intelligible differentia” between two different OBC candidates. 

These applications are now listed before the Supreme Court and are scheduled to be taken up next later this month.

title: Madanapalle weavers fight to keep their heritage alive amid economic hardship, fading tradition
author: K. Umashanker
content_html:
Before the sunrise, the quiet Neeruguttu Palle colony in Madanapalle begins to stir with the rhythmic sounds of a handloom. Inside a cramped room beneath a low roof, 58-year-old Subramanyam steps into the pit of his loom. His feet find the worn wooden treadles, and his hands take hold of the shuttle. The familiar khata-khat sounds mark the beginning of another 14-hour workday.

Outside his narrow wooden doorway, long hanks of crimson, teal, and gold silk thread are stretched between bamboo poles, drying in the cool morning air. Women walk past, carrying brass pots of starch water, while elderly men sit on stone ledges, carefully winding raw thread onto wooden bobbins.

But the handloom is no longer the only sound defining the colony. A few metres away, the rhythmic khata-khat gives way to the lounder hum of machinery. Inside a poorly lit concrete shed, 48-year-old Venkateswarulu supervises four motorised power looms clanking at top speed.

Between the two men, who are descendants of a long line of Rayalaseema weaving families, lies a striking contrast: one is tethered to the old ways of the slow precision of handlooms, while the other moves with the raw, unyielding speed of automated machinery.

Their experiences point to a wider trend documented in government records. According to official records under the One District One Product (ODOP) initiative, Madanapalle’s silk industry operates with nearly 7,500 active handloom units and over 8,000 weavers, supported by 35 primary cooperative societies. Additionally, a fast-growing network of around 200 power loom units is in operation. In reality, more than 50,000 people depend on this sector for their livelihoods.

Weaver Kavitha shows a saree woven on power loom at Neerugattu Palle in Madanapalle of Annamayya district. | Photo Credit: K. UMASHANKER

Undervalued

But the numbers only tell part of the story. For traditional handloom weavers, crafting a single six-yard saree—which fetches ₹15,000 to ₹25,000 in high-end shopping malls in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, or Chennai—requires nearly a full week of disciplined labour. Yet, what actually reaches the weaver’s hands is only a tiny fraction of that retail value, typically around ₹8,000 to ₹9,000 for materials and labour combined.

While the retail market undervalues their artistry, the local structural system squeezes their actual take-home earnings even further, reducing master craftsmanship to below-subsistence wages.

The unwritten rule here is that the master weavers and local middlemen supply the dyed silk yarn and metallic zari on credit, dictating the wage rate per piece. For a saree that takes five full days of hard manual labour to weave, a professional weaver carrying a State government ID card earns roughly ₹1,000 to ₹1,500—just ₹200 to ₹250 a day. This is noticeably less than what an unskilled daily wage worker earns at a local construction site or in the tomato loading yard at Madanapalle’s agricultural market.

For a community already navigating uncertain prices, unpredictable weather adds another layer of difficulty. The cottage industry is regularly disrupted by high monsoon humidity, which causes delicate threads to snap repeatedly. Weaving slows down, yet not a single rupee is added in extra pay. Furthermore, any rise in raw silk prices in the wholesale spot markets of major mulberry silk trading centres directly depresses weaver wages.

In such circumstances, the financial burden becomes severe for weavers families that rely heavily on a complex system of advance payments from master weavers and middlemen. A majority of weavers take small loans during lean agricultural seasons, daughters’ marriages, or medical emergencies—debts that effectively bind their labour for years.

“I took ₹25,000 for a hospital emergency, and suddenly I was tied to that trader’s order book for three years,” says Kavitha (35), a weaver who boils starch in a blackened clay pot behind the loom pit. “Even though we have the skill, we are not free to take our work to another trader who might offer ₹100 more per saree. Our old debt acts like handcuffs. In many cases, women like me work merely to pay interest, not to build a future,” she adds on a heavy note.

An elderly handloom weaver works under strained conditions at Neerugattu Palle in Madanapalle of the Annamayya district. | Photo Credit: K. UMASHANKER

Toll on well-being

The cost of the crisis for the weavers is not measured only in rupees but also in the physical toll that the arduous daily routine takes on their well-being. Health surveys across South Indian handloom belts reveal that eight out of ten pit-loom weavers suffer from severe back, neck, shoulder, and knee ailments caused by sitting crouched in narrow spaces for hours without proper spinal support.

“Constantly inhaling fine thread particles and micro-fibers damages our respiratory systems. Bronchitis and chronic coughs are common among our families,” says Siva, a young weaver.

For Ramachandra (56), the strain on the eyes is equally unforgiving. “We spend hours aligning microscopic silk threads under a single hanging 40-watt bulb. It causes intense tension and headaches, which eventually lead to premature eyesight decline and gradual vision loss by our 60s,” he says.

The weavers see these hardships as a lived reality, but the officials demand attention to these concerns. A revenue official in Madanapalle acknowledges that, to numb the constant aches in their joints and lumbar spine, several weavers turn to alcohol or smoking after long shifts. “Persistent joint pain often leads to severe substance dependency, which consumes their meagre earnings, triggers domestic conflict, and ruins their physical health. Declining health, mounting personal debt, and meagre incomes drive many weavers to silently abandon their looms and migrate elsewhere,” he says.

If the handloom takes its toll through long hours of repetitive work, the power loom brings its own set of risks. A power loom worker handles 35 to 50 meters of fabric daily per machine. Power loom weaver Rajasekhar, 46, says the primary concerns are not spinal posture or eye strain, but rather constant noise, heat, and machinery hazards. “Working near high-capacity motors without basic ear protection makes noise levels hazardous over time. My ears ring for hours after my shift ends. I started a decade ago, and the ringing has eventually faded—not because it stopped, but because my hearing has dulled. Now, I find it hard to hear my family at home unless they speak at a raised volume,” he adds.

The physical strain is only one dimension of the handloom’s predicament. In the market, it must also contend with the speed and scale of the power loom. “A machine-made imitation is ready in hours for a production cost of under ₹2,000. These products flood regional wholesale markets, threatening the survival of the handloom trade. While official Geographical Indication (GI) tags and the national Handloom Mark exist on paper to protect us, the reality on the ground is very different,” says Rajendra (38), who dropped out of a B. Tech programme to return to weaving.

The struggle at the loom points to a larger challenge for the sector, one that officials acknowledge. Assistant Director of the Handlooms & Textiles Department, Annamayya district, R. Pawan Kumar Reddy states that relentless physical labour and economic hardship are driving the younger generation away from the loom entirely.

“There is a severe shortage of young weavers in the handloom sector. To protect traditional artisans, the Central government strictly enforces regulations prohibiting power looms from manufacturing pure silk sarees without blending cotton or polyester. While violations occur, our inspection teams regularly monitor workstations to curb these practices,” Reddy says.

Financial concerns

He further adds that some families turn to loan apps and private lenders to manage financial stress, which damages their credit (CIBIL) scores and disqualifies them from government schemes like Mudra loans.

“Bankers strictly evaluate CIBIL scores before sanctioning loans. We continuously monitor industry stakeholders and remain available to address genuine trade challenges. In one instance, a weaver approached us after falling into a ₹10-lakh debt trap accrued entirely for personal reasons. In such cases, we are helpless, yet these situations contribute to the misconception that government support is minimal,” Reddy states.

Handloom weaver Chandrasekhar shows his product at Neerugattu Palle in Madanapalle of Annamayya district. | Photo Credit: K. UMASHANKER

‘Too little to offer’

The question of the industry’s future ultimately comes down to its next generation of workers. However, young people from across the silk town are opting for roles in retail stores, mobile repair shops, gig economy driving, or pursuing technical degrees over sitting in a family loom pit.

Mahesh, 21, a computer applications student, says he does not entertain the idea of taking up the trade. “My father worked surrounded by silk dust and deafening noise, but I get to sit in a bright classroom. I respect our family’s craft, but I see no viable future in work that demands so much physical sacrifice for so little financial security. I might consider the power loom sector someday, but not handlooms,” he says.

The decline of handloom pits is fraying the social fabric built over 150 years of Madanapalle’s silk heritage. For generations, weaving communities have operated as tight-knit social networks—sharing tasks like warping, sizing, dyeing, celebrating festivals together, and relying on informal local credit unions during tough seasons. As pit looms fall silent, these community support systems are gradually disappearing.

“Unfortunately, a stigma has attached to the weaver community—that we are drinkers, smokers, and lazy. While a small fraction may fit that description, the bad reputation burdens innocent, hardworking people as well,” says Sambasiva (40). He owns three handloom pits that consistently yield a monthly profit of ₹60,000. “If you are willing to work, there is an abundance of work. If you don’t want to work, you can invent a thousand excuses,” he adds.

On the other hand, local trade activists argue that existing welfare schemes fall short of preserving the industry. “We need direct, practical support on the ground—such as wage subsidies per meter, accessible healthcare clinics specialising in occupational hazards, free reading glasses, and strict legal enforcement against power loom design piracy. A steady, affordable supply of yarn and direct access to high-end urban markets are essential to free weavers from exploitative intermediaries,” says 60-year-old Chandrasekhar.

For now, the looms continue to move, even as the future they represent grows less certain.

title: Recommended to establish mandatory Statewide Differences/Disorders of Sex Development/intersex birth registry linked to civil registration, Gopi Shankar clarifies
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:
Gopi Shankar Madurai, Special Monitor for SOGIESC Rights, National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), has issued a clarification on a report headlined ‘Focus on gender non-conforming children’s needs: NHRC monitor’ published in The Hindu Thiruvananthapuram edition on Friday, and was based on a press release issued by the Kerala State Commission for Protection of Child Rights (KSCPCR). 

“The PRO of the KSCPCR has wrongly attributed my positions by treating Gender Non-Conforming Children (GNCC) as intersex/under the Differences/Disorders of Sex Development (DSD) category. This is factually and conceptually incorrect,” Gopi Shankar said.  

“I know the clear and fundamental difference between sex characteristics (intersex/DSD variations — innate biological variations in sex development) and gender identity/gender expression (which includes gender non-conforming children and transgender identities). These are distinct. Conflating them causes irreversible harm, stigma, and policy failure,” Gopi Shankar said.  

Referring to a court order, Gopi Shankar said non-consensual sex-selective or genital reconstructive surgery on intersex infants and children violates Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution. Surgery is permitted only if essential to save the child’s life, and only after opinion of a State-level Multidisciplinary Committee. The State, Gopi Shankar said, was directed to issue a regulating order within three months. 

Citing the document, Why the Kerala Government Must Implement the Kerala High Court Order on Intersex Infants and Children, Gopi Shankar said the court-mandated committee should be expanded into a permanent State DSD/Intersex Health Management Committee that must include a medical geneticist as a core member, along with paediatric endocrinologists, paediatric surgeons/urologists, child psychiatrists/psychologists, ethicists and intersex community representatives. 

Other recommendations include issuing evidence-based DSD management guidelines prioritising thorough diagnostic evaluation (including genetics), deferred non-urgent surgery, psychosocial support, and documented multidisciplinary review. Establishment of a mandatory Statewide DSD/intersex birth registry linked to civil registration is another recommendation.

title: Keralam seeks Sadya emoji, eyes global branding for traditional feast
author: Dhinesh Kallungal
content_html:
Although dieticians are a bit apprehensive about the high-calorie content of traditional Sadya (feast) of Keralam, a grand vegetarian feast served on a banana leaf comprising around 26 to 28 dishes, Kerala Tourism is exploring the possibility of turning the delicious Sadya of the State into an international brand.

Kerala Tourism has requested Apple CEO John Ternus, who assumed office on September 1, to include an emoji representing Keralam’s Sadya on iPhone. The request was made through the official social media handle of Kerala Tourism in response to a post by Mr. Ternus after assuming the office.

Speaking to The Hindu, a senior bureaucrat said, “We are not sure whether Apple would entertain such a request from Kerala Tourism. However, given the growing appeal of Sadya, especially during festival seasons such as Onam across the globe, we thought it would be a wise move to make such a request to the Apple CEO.”

Buzz on social media

Although the petition by Kerala Tourism has not evoked any response from the CEO so far, it has generated a buzz on social media platforms, with the move receiving widespread support from netizens as Sadya is a hallmark of festivals as well as various religious ceremonies and wedding celebrations in the State.

According to James Kodianthara, a tourism expert and former chairperson of the Kerala chapter of the Indian Association of Tour Operators (IATO), Sadya is definitely a grand product from Keralam that could be marketed as an international brand across the globe.

“There are a lot of examples across the world, like steak in American cuisine and pork knuckle in Czech cuisine, which have brought fame and international recognition to destinations. Perhaps, after Kathakali and snakeboat regatta, Sadya can fetch international spotlight to Keralam,” said Mr. Kodianthara.

Main dishes

A lot of airlines serving southern India serve Sadya aboard their flights, especially during festival occasions such as Onam. The feast includes dishes such as Kaalan made with coconut; cucumber Pachadi, a garnished salad; and Puli Inji, a sweet and tangy ginger-based chutney; along with Payasams and other dishes.

Meanwhile, Dr. Anupa Jose, a dietician, attached to a private clinic, said that although Sadya is an integral part of Keralites' lives, the amount of rice served on the banana leaf should be reduced, given the high-calorie content of the traditional feast. Instead, curries prepared with legumes and lentils should be given equal prominence in the feast to limit total calorie intake to less than 1,000 while ensuring adequate protein.
